unit: cents of each DSP dollar reaching the consumer
text: The ANA's programmatic transparency study found about 36 cents of every dollar entering a demand-side platform reached a consumer — transaction costs took 29 cents and media-productivity loss (non-viewable, invalid traffic, unmeasurable and made-for-advertising inventory) took 35 cents. Of the roughly $88B open-web programmatic pool the study sized, the ANA identified about $22B — a quarter — as recoverable efficiency gain; that is not the same as the 64 cents on the dollar that fails to reach a consumer, which on the same pool is about $56B. Made-for-advertising sites absorbed about 15% of spend on the June 2023 first look, and $10B of the $88B pool (11.4%) on the December full report. BASIS CAVEAT: the study's participants are 21 US marketers, but the $88B pool is described as the open-web programmatic market excluding $20.3B of CTV, and whether that pool is US-only or global could not be confirmed from a reachable primary source. Do not treat $88B as a US total.

text: Nobody in this era was hired to make advertisements. The agency was invented as a space broker: Volney B. Palmer opened in Philadelphia in 1841-42 and was paid by publishers, taking roughly 25 percent of what he sold. By the 1850s a dozen rivals each claimed to represent every paper of importance, and the commission an agent could extract ranged from about 10 to 50 percent. George P. Rowell (Boston, 1865) industrialised the model by buying space in bulk and reselling it in slices. The decisive break came in 1875, when N. W. Ayer & Son offered advertisers the 'open contract': the agent would work for the buyer, disclose the rate, and take a fixed percentage. Once the agent's income no longer depended on hiding the price, the agency had to sell something else - market research (Ayer's Nichols-Shepard study, 1880), then copy and art (from the 1890s). By 1904-07 Lord & Thomas under Albert Lasker had turned copy into the product, hiring John E. Kennedy ('advertising is salesmanship in print') and then Claude Hopkins, who tested headlines against keyed coupons. The full-service agency, the pitch, and the fixed commission all existed before 1917; the trade body that froze them, the 4As, was founded in June of that year.
